Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Newsfile to discuss Traffitech-GH fines, drug busts and Parliament’s continued absence of Asante Akyem North MP Source : Prince Adu-Owusu 6 November 2026 8:13pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
This Saturday’s edition of Newsfile on JoyNews will examine three major issues dominating Ghana’s public discourse, as host Samson Lardy Anyenini leads discussions on road safety enforcement, the fight against drug trafficking and developments in Parliament.
The programme, scheduled for Saturday, November 7, 2026, from 8:00 a.m. to 12 noon, will scrutinise the implementation of the Traffitech-GH system, renewed drug seizures and the continued absence of the Member of Parliament for Asante Akyem North from parliamentary proceedings.
The first major issue will focus on TraffiTech-GH and whether the new automated traffic enforcement system will deliver safer roads or impose unfair financial burdens on motorists. The system, which became operational on November 1, 2026, is intended to strengthen compliance with road traffic regulations through technology-driven monitoring and enforcement.
However, its introduction has attracted criticism from commercial transport operators, who accuse the government of prioritising fines while failing to address the occupation of designated bus stops and pedestrian walkways by traders. The National Road Safety Authority (NRSA) has also raised concerns about faulty traffic lights, missing road signs and faded road markings, warning that these deficiencies could undermine the effectiveness of the system.
With the Ghana Police Service urging motorists to verify traffic violation notices before making payments, the programme will examine whether the system is adequately designed to improve road safety while ensuring fairness and transparency in its enforcement.
The discussion will also turn to the growing number of drug seizures linked to Ghana and questions about the effectiveness of the country's border security systems. Recent developments have renewed concerns about Ghana's role in international drug trafficking networks, particularly following the seizure of 46.7 kilogrammes of cocaine at the Rafic Hariri International Airport in Beirut, Lebanon, in a consignment that originated from Accra.
The Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC) has defended its decision to allow a suspected trafficker to travel to Lebanon, explaining that it was part of a controlled-delivery operation intended to identify and arrest other members of the international trafficking network. Three foreign nationals have subsequently been arrested in Ghana in connection with the shipment.
The concerns have been compounded by a fresh interception of approximately 4.8 tonnes of suspected marijuana by the Ghana Navy at the Volta Lake estuary near Ada, with the consignment allegedly destined for Nigeria.
The Minority in Parliament has meanwhile demanded accountability from President John Mahama over what it describes as failures in the country's border protection arrangements. It has also renewed calls for a parliamentary inquiry into the major drug seizures, raising questions about port security, intelligence coordination and possible institutional weaknesses.
Newsfile will interrogate whether the successive seizures reflect failures in Ghana's border controls or form part of coordinated operations to dismantle international drug trafficking networks.
Another significant issue will be Parliament's resumption for the third meeting of the Second Session of the Ninth Parliament without the Member of Parliament for Asante Akyem North, Ohene Kwame Frimpong.
The MP remains in custody in the Netherlands following his arrest at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport in May 2026, in connection with a United States extradition request over allegations involving romance scams and money laundering. Two applications for bail have reportedly been unsuccessful, with his extradition hearing scheduled for November 18, 2026.
His prolonged absence has raised questions about the constitutional provisions governing an MP's failure to attend parliamentary sittings and whether his continued detention could put his parliamentary seat at risk.
Private legal practitioner Martin Kpebu has cited a 2008 Court of Appeal ruling involving former Nkoranza North MP Eric Amoateng, arguing that the precedent could have implications for Mr Frimpong's situation, particularly regarding the constitutional requirement for written permission from the Speaker for prolonged absence.
The Majority, however, maintains that the seat should not be declared vacant while the MP remains presumed innocent and has not been convicted of any offence.
The programme will examine the legal and constitutional implications of his continued absence and what it means for parliamentary representation in Asante Akyem North.
With these issues commanding national attention, Saturday's Newsfile promises a robust examination of road safety, institutional accountability, national security and constitutional governance.
Join Samson Lardy Anyenini and his panellists this Saturday, November 7, from 8:00 a.m. to 12 noon on JoyNews and JoyFM 99.7.
